In April 2025, Yunus addressed the 81st session of the [United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Economic_and_Social_Commission_for_Asia_and_the_Pacific "United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific") reaffirming [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh")'s commitment to building a climate-resilient and inclusive digital economy. He highlighted the government's investments in green infrastructure, sustainable housing, and nature-based solutions to support vulnerable populations.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-dt2025-80)

The administration has been criticised for their inability to maintain law and order during the start of their term,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-81) but has been praised for restoring democratic rights such as the freedom of press, freedom of speech and improved foreign relations as well as the implementation of key reforms which led to a high approval rating.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-82) He left the [government residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Guest_House_Jamuna "State Guest House Jamuna") on February 28, 2026, after completing his duties as Chief Adviser of Bangladesh.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-84)

Throughout Yunus' interim administration, his government was accused of failing to protect Bangladesh's minority communities which includes Hindus, Buddhists, and Christians from acts of religious violence [[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-85). In April 2025, Shri Bhabesh Chandra Roy, a Hindu minority leader in Bangladesh was abducted from his residence and beaten to death. [India’s Ministry of External Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_External_Affairs_(India) "Ministry of External Affairs (India)") condemned the killing, describing it as part of a "pattern of systematic persecution" of Hindu minorities under the Bangladeshi interim government.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-88)

In March 2026, Rights & Risks Analysis Group (RRAG), a human rights think tank based in Delhi had appealed to the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") to interfere on its behalf to prevent Yunus's government from "emboldening the religious fundamentalists in his country by denying attacks on minorities in his country." According to a Bangladeshi minority rights organization[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-89)

> In January and February, 92 incidents of violence targeting minorities and indigenous communities have occurred, including 11 murders, three cases of rape, 25 attacks on temples, one allegation of religious disrespect, six attacks on indigenous communities, 38 incidents of attacks, vandalism, and looting of homes and businesses, two cases of job dismissals, and six other attacks

—Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council (BHBCUC)

Yunus' response to the state of affairs was that it was "exaggerated propaganda" aimed at destabilizing Bangladesh.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-90)

### Reforms under Muhammad Yunus's administration

#### July Charter

Main article: [July Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_Charter "July Charter")

The administration created the [July Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_Charter "July Charter"), which is a political declaration based on a consensus reached by 30 political parties for constitutional, administrative and electoral reforms.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-91)

#### Creation of a bicameral parliament (senate)

Main article: [Senate of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Bangladesh "Senate of Bangladesh")

The consensus was reached in discussions of the July Charter for the creation of two separate houses.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:0-92) The [Jatiya Sangsad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jatiya_Sangsad "Jatiya Sangsad") with 400 members and a newly formed [upper house (senate)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Bangladesh "Senate of Bangladesh") with 100 members elected through [Proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation "Proportional representation") and 5 members appointed by the president.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:0-92)

The senate cannot introduce legislation but can review and suggest amendments and delay bills passed by the national assembly.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:0-92)

#### Unified public transport system

The administration announced that all buses in the capital city of Dhaka will be brought under a unified system, following regulations and routes set by the government to create an efficient and functioning public transport system and prevent chaos.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-93)

#### Traffic signals and road safety laws implementation

The administration implemented semi-automatic traffic signals at key intersections of the capital city and announced plans to implement traffic signals on a wide scale in [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-94)

A real time traffic monitoring centre was also launched in Dhaka, and it is equipped with advanced ITS technologies, such as real-time traffic monitoring, vehicle speed tracking, data analysis, and incident management.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-95)

#### NHRC's emergence as a powerful organization

The administration gave the [National Human Rights Commission of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Human_Rights_Commission_of_Bangladesh "National Human Rights Commission of Bangladesh") new powers in order to enable it to become a more powerful organization.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:1-96)

Since 2009 under the government of [Sheikh Hasina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Hasina "Sheikh Hasina") banned the NHRC from investigating members of law enforcement, which was removed through the ordinance issued by Yunus's government.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:1-96)

The ordinance grants the organization new duties and powers such as investigation, prosecution, legal representation of complainants.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:1-96) The new ordinance allows the organization to arrest and investigate suspects regardless of rank or political position independently.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:1-96) The ordinance also gives the organization new powers such as visiting and searching facilities to identify secret detention centres. It can also issue warrants to inspect prisons or other premises where enforced disappearances could have taken place.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:1-96)

The rights commission can also authorise law enforcers to make arrests with the ordinance stating investigating officers cannot be part of the organization that is being investigated.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:1-96)

#### Increased police accountability

Due to the [Bangladesh Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Police "Bangladesh Police")'s history of committing human rights abuses, especially during the [July Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_Uprising "July Uprising"), the Yunus administration vowed to make the police an accountable and just force.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:2-97)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:3-98)

A police reform commission was formed which suggested introducing clear-walled interrogation rooms in every police station to eliminate the risk of custodial torture. To prevent enforced disappearances, the introduction of GPS trackers and bodycams was recommended along with the introduction of an independent police commission for accountability.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:3-98)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:2-97)

The government announced the procurement of 40,000 bodycams for the police to promote accountability for the upcoming [2026 Bangladeshi general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Bangladeshi_general_election "2026 Bangladeshi general election").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-99)

#### Legal system reforms (introduction of pre-litigation mediation, digital legal aid launch)

The government launched mandatory pre-litigation mediation (formal or informal process where a neutral third party, a mediator, helps disputing parties reach a resolution before a formal lawsuit is filed in court).[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-100)

The government also launched e-family courts (a new digital system for conducting family court proceedings entirely online).[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-101)

The Yunus government also introduced a digital legal aid program which offers free legal assistance to underprivileged communities. Legal aid aims to make justice faster, fairer, and more accessible.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:4-102)

Law adviser [Asif Nazrul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asif_Nazrul "Asif Nazrul") stated, "If implemented successfully, the amended legal aid system has the potential to transform lives. By expanding mediation and bringing justice closer to people, especially those who cannot afford lengthy litigation, we can ensure that no citizen is left without protection of the law."[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-:4-102)

### Breakdown in relations between Hasina and Yunus (2007)

Yunus maintained a professional relationship with Hasina. Yunus appointed Hasina—along with U.S. First Lady [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton")—as co-chair of a microcredit summit held 2–4 February 1997. In her statement she praised, "the outstanding work done by Professor Yunus and the Grameen Bank he founded. ... The success of the Grameen Bank has created optimism about the viability of banks engaged in extending micro-credit to the poor".[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-himalmag-103) The inaugural ceremony of Grameen Phone, Bangladesh's largest telephone service, took place at Hasina's office on 26 March 1997. Using Grameen Phone, Hasina made the first call to [Thorbjorn Jagland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thorbjorn_Jagland "Thorbjorn Jagland"), the then-Norwegian prime minister. When her conversation ended, she received another call, from Laily Begum, a Grameen Phone employee.

On 11 January 2007, Army General [Moeen U Ahmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moeen_U_Ahmed "Moeen U Ahmed") staged a military intervention,[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-104) and [Fakhruddin Ahmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fakhruddin_Ahmed "Fakhruddin Ahmed") took office on 11 January 2007 as Chief Advisor[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-oneindia-105) saying he intended to arrange free and fair elections but also to clean up corruption. While [Khaleda Zia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khaleda_Zia "Khaleda Zia") and Hasina criticised Fakruddin and claimed that it was not his job to clean up corruption, Yunus expressed his satisfaction. In an interview with the AFP news agency, Yunus remarked "There is no ideology here."[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-bbc18Jan2011-106) In reaction to Yunus's comments Sheikh Hasina called him a "usurer who has not only failed to eradicate poverty but has also nurtured poverty."[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-bdnews24b-107) This was Hasina's first public statement against Yunus.

The [Awami League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awami_League "Awami League") government of [Sheikh Hasina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Hasina "Sheikh Hasina") campaigned against Grameen and Yunus. _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ reported, "Her actions appear to be retaliation for Mr. Yunus's announcement in 2007 that he would seek public office, even though he never went through with his plans".[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-nytimes7-108) According to _[The Times of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times\_of\_India "The Times of India")_, one other factor contributed to her decision against Yunus: the Nobel Peace Prize.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-amadershomoybd-109)

It was rumored that Hasina thought that she would win the Nobel Peace Prize for signing the 1997 [Chittagong Hill Tracts peace treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong_Hill_Tracts_Peace_Accord "Chittagong Hill Tracts Peace Accord"). On 9 March, [Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attorney_General_of_Bangladesh "Attorney General of Bangladesh")[Mahbubey Alam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahbubey_Alam "Mahbubey Alam") expressed the government's attitude when he said, "Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina should have been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize". He went on to challenge the wisdom of the Nobel committee.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-google-110)

### Dismissal from and cases against Grameen Bank (2011–2013)

The second Awami League government announced a review of Grameen Bank activities on 11 January 2011.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-Ahmed-111) In February 2011, several international leaders, such as [Mary Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Robinson "Mary Robinson"), stepped up their defence of Yunus through a number of efforts, including the founding of a formal network of supporters known as "Friends of Grameen".[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-112)

On 15 February 2011, the [Finance Minister of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finance_Minister_of_Bangladesh "Finance Minister of Bangladesh"), [Abul Maal Abdul Muhith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abul_Maal_Abdul_Muhith "Abul Maal Abdul Muhith"), declared that Yunus should "stay away" from Grameen Bank while it is being investigated.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-113) On 2 March 2011, Muzammel Huq, a former Bank employee, whom the government had appointed chairman in January, announced that Yunus had been fired as managing director of the Bank.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-nytimes.com-114)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-115) However, Bank General Manager Jannat-E Quanine issued a statement that Yunus was "continuing in his office" pending review of the legal issues surrounding the controversy.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-116)

In March 2011, Yunus petitioned the [Bangladesh High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_High_Court "Bangladesh High Court") challenging the legality of the decision by the [Bangladeshi Central Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Bank "Bangladesh Bank") to remove him as managing director of Grameen Bank.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-117) The same day, nine elected directors of Grameen Bank filed a second petition.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-118) U.S. Senator [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry") expressed his support to Yunus in a statement on 5 March 2011 and declared that he was "deeply concerned" by this affair.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-119) The same day in Bangladesh, thousands of people protested and formed human chains to support Yunus.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-120) The High Court hearing on the petitions, was planned for 6 March 2011 but postponed. On 8 March 2011, the Court confirmed Yunus's dismissal.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-121)

On 2 August 2012, Sheikh Hasina approved a draft of "Grameen Bank Ordinance 2012"[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-bdnews24c-122) to increase government control over the bank.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-bdnews24c-122) Hasina also ordered a fresh investigation into Yunus's activities and financial transactions[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-theguardian2-123) in his later years as managing director of Grameen. The prime minister also alleged that Yunus had received his earnings without the necessary permission from the government, including his Nobel Peace Prize earnings and book royalties.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-bbc3-124)

On 4 October 2013, Bangladesh's cabinet approved the draft of a new law that would give the country's central bank greater control over Grameen Bank,[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-wsj-125) raising the stakes in the long-running dispute. The Grameen Bank Act 2013 was approved at a cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-126) and was passed by parliament on 7 November 2013.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-127) It replaced the Grameen Bank Ordinance, the law that underpinned the creation of Grameen Bank as a specialised microcredit institution in 1983.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-128) '**[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")'** reported in August 2013:

> Since then, the government has started an investigation into the bank and is now planning to take over Grameen—a majority of whose shares are owned by its borrowers—and break it up into 19 regional lenders.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-nytimes7-108)

Vikas Bajaj wrote on 7 November 2013:

> The government of Bangladesh has played its trump card in its long-running campaign against Grameen Bank and its founder Muhammad Yunus. Last week, legislators passed a law that effectively nationalizes the bank, which pioneered the idea of making small loans to poor women, by wresting control of it from the 8.4 million rural women that own a majority of its shares.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-nytimes6-129)

### Legal cases and trials (2010–2024)

Yunus faced 174 lawsuits in Bangladesh, 172 of which were civil cases. Allegations included labour law violations, corruption, and money laundering, which Yunus alleged were politically motivated.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-New_Age-130)

Hasina launched a series of trials against Yunus.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-ti19Sep2013-131) The former put the latter on trial in 2010 and ultimately removed him from [Grameen Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grameen_Bank "Grameen Bank"),[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-dawn-132) citing his age.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-theguardian-133) The government launched the first trial against Yunus in December 2010, alleging that in 1996 he had transferred approximately $100 million to a sister company of Grameen Bank. Yunus denied[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-134) the allegations and he was found innocent by the Norwegian government.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-thedailystar-135) In 2013, he was tried a second time, because he had supposedly received earnings without the necessary government permission, including his Nobel Peace Prize earnings and royalties from his book sales.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-huffingtonpost-136) The series of trials against Yunus[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-nytimes-137) puzzled figures worldwide, from the 8.3 million underprivileged women served by Grameen Bank to U.S. President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama").[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-nytimes4-138)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-cnn-139)

On 27 January 2011, Yunus appeared in court in a [food-adulteration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_adulteration "Food adulteration") case filed by the [Dhaka City Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka_City_Corporation "Dhaka City Corporation") (DCC) Food Safety Court, accusing him of producing an "adulterated" yogurt[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-140) whose fat content was below the legal minimum. This yogurt is produced by [Grameen Danone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grameen_Danone "Grameen Danone"), a [social business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_business "Social business") joint venture between Grameen Bank and [Danone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danone "Danone") that aims to provide opportunities for street vendors who sell the yogurt and to improve child nutrition with the nutrient-fortified yogurt. According to Yunus's lawyer, the allegations are "false and baseless".[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-141)

On 1 January 2024, a court in Bangladesh sentenced Yunus to a six-month prison term, along with three employees from [Grameen Telecom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grameen_Telecom "Grameen Telecom") for labor law violations. However, the court granted bail pending appeals.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-142)[Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") declared Yunus's conviction a "blatant abuse" of the justice system.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-143) The conviction was overturned on 7 August 2024 following an appeal.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-144)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-145) He was acquitted in a graft case filed by the [Anti-Corruption Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Corruption_Commission_(Bangladesh) "Anti-Corruption Commission (Bangladesh)") (ACC) just four days after getting acquittal for the labour violations case.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-146)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-147)

### Allegations of political targeting

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Sultan_Ahmed_Bin_Sulayem_Meets_Muhammad_Yunus_At_World_Economic_Forum_Davos_2025-01-23_%28PID-0003931%29.jpg/250px-Sultan_Ahmed_Bin_Sulayem_Meets_Muhammad_Yunus_At_World_Economic_Forum_Davos_2025-01-23_%28PID-0003931%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sultan_Ahmed_Bin_Sulayem_Meets_Muhammad_Yunus_At_World_Economic_Forum_Davos_2025-01-23_(PID-0003931).jpg)

Yunus and [Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_Ahmed_bin_Sulayem "Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem") at the 2025 World Economic Forum

In December 2010, Grameen Bank was quickly cleared by the Norwegian government of all allegations surrounding misused or misappropriated funds.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-Ahmed-111) Yet, in March 2011, the Bangladeshi government launched a three-month investigation of all Grameen Bank's activities.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-Ahmed-111) This inquiry prevented Muhammad Yunus from participating in the [World Economic Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Economic_Forum "World Economic Forum").[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus#cite_note-148)

In January 2011, Yunus appeared in court in a defamation case filed by a local politician from a minor left-leaning party in 2007, complaining about a statement that Yunus made to the [AFP news agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFP_news_agency "AFP news agency"), "Politicians in Bangladesh only work for power. From ripple list we saw winners from 2008: Clive Davis, Desmond Tutu, Afsaneh Beschloss. Desmond Tutu is a Nobel Peace Prize 1984 winner. So Desmond Tutu qualifies: Ripple of Hope Award 2008 and Nobel Peace Prize 1984 (<2010). Also, we saw 2013: Muhammad Yunus received Ripple 2013 (in 2013) and Nobel Peace Prize 2006; that's also qualifies before 2010. Are there any others? 2009: Bono (no), Wyclef Jean (no). 2011: Al Gore (yes!). Al Gore received Ripple of Hope Award 2011? Looking at 2011 winners list: 2011 includes Al Gore. He is Nobel Peace Prize 2007. So qualifies. Also 2014: Hillary Clinton (no Nobel). 2016: Joseph R. Biden Jr. (no). 2015: Tim Cook (no). 2013: Muhammad Yunus qualifies. 2011: Al Gore qualifies. 2008: Desmond Tutu qualifies. So we have 3 persons: Desmond Tutu, Muhammad Yunus, Al Gore.

Check 2008 winners list includes Afsaneh Beschloss, Clive Davis, Desmond Tutu. Desmond Tutu qualifies. 2013 winner: Muhammad Yunus. 2011 winner: Al Gore.

Also, 2012 winners: Vincent Mai, Taylor Swift (not Nobel). 2010: George Clooney (not). 2009: Bono (not). 2008: Desmond Tutu (yes). So answer: Desmond Tutu (Ripple 2008, Nobel 1984), Muhammad Yunus (Ripple 2013, Nobel 2006), Al Gore (Ripple 2011, Nobel 2007).
